name: Brali Flagship 100
description: A deterministic high-trust core selected from the Brali trusted Protocol Feed. Start Here anchors and the fixed Gold 20 evaluation cohort are retained so reviewed retrieval contracts cannot disappear as the trusted pool grows.
selection_rule: Trusted feed only; complete core content; safety-sensitive items require reviewed evidence with a source URL; retain Start Here and Gold 20 evaluation candidates; then deterministic quality and diversity ranking.
caveat: Flagship status is a retrieval and editorial quality signal. Gold 20 candidate retention preserves evaluation coverage but is not Gold approval, and it does not mean every protocol has the same evidence strength or that Brali provides medical advice.

entries.title: Work in Focused 25-Minute Intervals (pomodoros) Followed by a 5-Minute Break
entries.description: Work in focused 25-minute intervals (Pomodoros) followed by a 5-minute break. After four Pomodoros, take a longer break.
entries.action: Pick one concrete outcome, work on it for one 25-minute focus block, take a short break, and then decide whether another block is useful. Treat 25 minutes as a starting setting, not a scientifically optimal duration.
entries.check_in: Did I work on the intended outcome? What interrupted me, and should the next focus block be shorter, the same, or longer?

entries.title: Separate Outcomes From Actions You Can Control
entries.description: Draw two circles; one for factors you can control and another for those you cannot. Set clear, achievable goals based on what’s within your control.
entries.action: Write down one concern, separate the outcome from the actions you can take, convert anything you can influence into one concrete behavior, and choose the next useful action without pretending you control the final result.
entries.check_in: What part of this situation was actually mine to act on, what remained outside my control, and did the sorting help me choose a clearer next step?

entries.title: Start a Morning Stretch Routine
entries.description: Begin each day with a 10-minute stretch routine, increasing to 20 minutes over time.
entries.action: Use a short, gentle flexibility routine as a morning movement cue if that timing suits you. Move slowly only as far as is comfortable, start with a few simple movements, and build up gradually rather than forcing a fixed 10-to-20-minute progression.
entries.check_in: Did the movements feel comfortable and controlled? Did I stop or modify anything that caused pain or made me feel unwell, and is this routine still appropriate for me?

entries.title: Spend Each Week Focused on a Single Theme
entries.description: Spend each week focused on a single theme. Immerse yourself in everything related to that topic through reading, watching, and activities.
entries.action: Choose one narrow learning theme for the week, define one visible result for Friday, and complete at least one small practice rep on each day you work on it.
entries.check_in: Did I complete one practice rep? What was the main friction, and what should I change for the next rep?

entries.title: Do Active Listening Exercises
entries.description: Practice active listening by summarizing and repeating back what the other person has said to confirm understanding.
entries.action: In one conversation, wait until the other person finishes a thought, paraphrase the main point in your own words, invite correction, and ask one open question before offering advice or changing the topic.
entries.check_in: Did I summarize before responding? Was my summary accepted or corrected, and what did the correction teach me?

entries.title: In a Group, Write Down Ideas and Pass Them Around for Others to Build
entries.description: In a group, write down ideas and pass them around for others to build on.
entries.action: Give the group one clear question, let everyone write ideas silently, pass the ideas to another person to add or change them, and delay discussion until the group has built several options.
entries.check_in: Did everyone get a chance to contribute before discussion? Which idea became more useful after another person built on it, and what should the group test next?

entries.title: When Faced with a Problem, Start by Making an Educated Guess About the Cause
entries.description: When faced with a problem, start by making an educated guess about the cause. Write down your hypothesis and what you expect to happen if it’s true.
entries.action: When a work problem is unclear, write one plausible explanation, state what you would expect to observe if it were true, run the smallest safe check that could change your mind, and update the hypothesis from the result.
entries.check_in: What did I expect to observe, what actually happened, and what changed in my explanation after the test?

entries.title: Use WOOP to Turn a Wish Into an If-Then Plan
entries.description: Use a Wish, desired Outcome, likely internal Obstacle, and a concrete if-then Plan to make one meaningful goal easier to act on. Treat the method as a self-regulation tool, not a guarantee of goal achievement.
entries.action: Choose one meaningful and reasonably feasible wish. Describe the outcome you want, identify an internal obstacle that could derail you, then write: If I notice this obstacle, then I will take this specific action. Try the plan in real life and revise it if the cue or response is not useful.
entries.check_in: Did the obstacle actually appear, did my if-then response help me act, and what should I keep or change next time?

entries.title: Plan Your Workday in Three Simple Blocks
entries.description: Split the day into a few broad work blocks and choose a small set of clear outcomes for each. Use three blocks and up to three tasks per block as a template, not a rule.
entries.action: Divide the workday into up to three broad blocks. Give each block one to three clear outcomes that fit the time you actually have. Replan when meetings, urgent work, or delays change the day.
entries.check_in: Did the blocks help me choose what mattered, and was any block overloaded, too vague, or too rigid?

entries.title: Use a Short Timebox for a Rough First Pass
entries.description: Give a low-risk task a shorter-than-usual timebox, define what a useful first pass must contain, and reduce scope instead of pretending you can preserve everything by working faster.
entries.action: Pick a low-risk task where an imperfect first pass is useful. Set a short timebox, define the minimum useful output, and decide what you will leave for later. Stop or reassess when the timebox ends.
entries.check_in: Did the timebox help me make useful scope decisions, and what should be improved before this work is actually finished or shared?

entries.title: Alternate Focused Work With Real Breaks
entries.description: Use a protected focus block followed by a real break, then adjust the length to your task, energy, and schedule instead of treating 90/30 as a biological rule.
entries.action: Choose one important task, protect a focus block from avoidable interruptions, then step away for a real break. Adjust both periods to your workload and energy rather than forcing a fixed 90/30 schedule.
entries.check_in: Was the focus block long enough to make progress, did the break actually feel like a break, and what duration would fit the next cycle better?

entries.title: Do a Short Desk Reset
entries.description: Set a timer for 2 minutes and tidy up your workspace. Put away unnecessary items and clear some space for your tasks.
entries.action: Set a short timer and tidy one small part of your workspace. Make only obvious moves, then stop before tidying turns into a larger task.
entries.check_in: Is the workspace easier to use now, and did I stop before tidying became a new form of procrastination?

entries.title: Active Recall: Close the Notes and Make Memory Work
entries.description: Before rereading, hide the source and try to produce the answer from memory. Then check it, fix the misses, and practice application separately if the real goal is solving, speaking, writing, or doing. Familiarity feels nice; retrieval tells you what is actually available without the page in front of you.
entries.action: Choose a small set of material you want to retain. Hide the source and answer a question, explain the idea, or write what you remember. Check immediately enough to catch errors and repair them. Then, if success means solving, writing, speaking, calculating, or performing, practice that outcome too. Memory practice is useful; it is not a teleportation device to skill.
entries.check_in: What could I retrieve without looking? What was missing or wrong? If the real goal is application, could I actually use the knowledge in a relevant task?

entries.title: Try Quiet Wakeful Rest After Learning
entries.description: After learning declarative material you want to remember, try a short period of quiet, minimally stimulating wakeful rest before switching to another demanding task. Treat it as a personal memory experiment, not a general learning upgrade or a universal ten-minute rule.
entries.action: When you finish a focused memory-heavy learning episode, put aside the material and spend a brief period awake in a quiet, low-stimulation setting. Avoid immediately switching to another cognitively demanding task. Choose a duration that is practical for you, then return to normal activity. Do not use the pause as a substitute for self-testing, active review, or other learning methods.
entries.check_in: What did I learn, did I actually create a low-interference pause afterward, and when I checked later did recall seem better, unchanged, or worse than usual?

entries.title: Practice One Small Language Skill for a Short Session
entries.description: Use a short study session to practice one narrow language skill such as recalling a few words, listening to a short clip, or speaking a brief response. Ten minutes is a convenient starting point, not a required dose.
entries.action: Pick one narrow language task, such as reviewing a few phrases, listening to a short clip, reading a small passage, or recording a brief spoken answer. Practice for a short session and finish with one note about what to revisit next.
entries.check_in: What did I practice, what could I recall or understand without help, and what is the next small thing worth repeating?

entries.title: Check Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How
entries.description: Before an important operational message, check whether the reader has the people, action, place, timing, reason, and next-step details they actually need.
entries.action: Review an important operational message using six questions: Who? What? Where? When? Why? How? Add only the missing details the reader needs to act, then send the shortest version that is still clear.
entries.check_in: Could the reader act without guessing, and did I include any detail that was unnecessary or sensitive?

entries.title: Ask Why Until a Goal Becomes Clearer
entries.description: Use repeated why questions to examine what is behind a goal, then turn the useful insight into a next step. Five questions are a prompt, not a requirement or a guarantee of finding one root cause.
entries.action: Write one goal or problem, ask why it matters, and continue asking why while each answer adds something useful. Stop when the answers become repetitive, speculative, or split into different causes. Then choose one next step or one assumption to check.
entries.check_in: Did the questions reveal a useful reason, assumption, or constraint, and what will I do or verify next?

entries.title: Compare Two Approaches and Learn From the Result
entries.description: When a decision is reversible, compare two approaches around one clear question, keep the outcome you care about visible, and avoid treating a tiny informal comparison as statistical proof.
entries.action: Choose one reversible decision, define what you want to learn, compare two approaches as fairly as you can, and record the outcome before deciding what to try next. Use proper experimental design when the result needs statistical confidence.
entries.check_in: What changed between the two approaches, what outcome did I observe, and is the evidence strong enough to act or only strong enough to suggest another test?

entries.title: Protect Enough Sleep Opportunity and Track Daytime Function
entries.description: If your sleep is routinely short, protect a realistic window that gives you enough opportunity to sleep and observe simple trends in sleep timing and daytime alertness. Do not deliberately restrict sleep to search for an 'optimal' number or treat one bad night as a result.
entries.action: Choose a bedtime-to-wake window that fits your obligations and gives you a reasonable opportunity for enough sleep. For a week or two, record only a few things: roughly when you tried to sleep, when you got up, whether the night was unusually disrupted, and how alert or sleepy you felt during the day. Look for repeated patterns, not single-night scores. Change one practical constraint at a time, such as moving bedtime earlier when your current schedule routinely leaves too little time for sleep.
entries.check_in: Did I give myself enough opportunity to sleep, what did my actual sleep/wake pattern look like, and was daytime alertness broadly better, unchanged, or worse over several days?

entries.title: Take a Short Walk When Stress Builds
entries.description: Whenever stress hits, take a quick 10-minute walk—whether it’s outside, around a park, or just circling your office.
entries.action: When stress is building, consider a short, comfortable walk if walking is safe and practical for you. Treat ten minutes as a convenient boundary, not a medically proven dose. If a greener route is just as easy and safe, prefer it as a reasonable experiment rather than making a special trip. Then notice whether you feel any different before returning to the next task.
entries.check_in: Did I take the walk? Was the route ordinary or relatively green? How did my stress or tension feel before and after, and did I return more able to continue the next task?

entries.title: Use the 20-20-20 Rule for Screen Breaks
entries.description: When you spend a long time looking at screens, take a short distance-viewing break: about every 20 minutes, look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds.
entries.action: During long periods of screen use, take a short visual break about every 20 minutes and look at something about 20 feet away for 20 seconds. Use the reminder as a simple screen-rest cue, not as a treatment or a substitute for eye care.
entries.check_in: Did I take regular screen breaks, and are eye strain, dryness, headaches, or blurred vision still bothering me enough that I should discuss them with an eye-care professional?

entries.title: Turn One Routine Exchange into a Genuine Micro-Conversation
entries.description: When the situation is relaxed and the other person seems willing, make one routine exchange slightly more human: eye contact, a real greeting, or a brief conversation. Treat it as a small social opportunity, not a cure for loneliness.
entries.action: Pick an ordinary low-pressure interaction that already needs to happen: buying coffee, greeting a neighbor, talking to a receptionist, or another brief exchange. If the context is appropriate, make eye contact, greet the person, and add one natural sentence or question. Keep it short and responsive to the other person's cues. If they are busy, uncomfortable, or not interested, let the interaction stay efficient.
entries.check_in: Did the interaction feel more connected without becoming intrusive, and did the other person seem willing to engage?

entries.title: Use Your Senses to Return to the Present
entries.description: Spend 3–5 minutes focusing on your senses. Notice what you see, hear, smell, feel, and taste. Gently redirect your attention whenever your mind wanders.
entries.action: Pause somewhere safe and deliberately notice what is happening around you right now. Choose a few sights, sounds, textures, smells or tastes and describe them simply. When your attention drifts into planning, worry or commentary, notice that and gently return to one sensory detail.
entries.check_in: What did I notice, how easy or difficult was it to return attention to the present, and did this feel useful enough to try again?

entries.title: Match Feedback to the Revision Target
entries.description: When revising a student or learning-focused draft, decide whether the current pass targets surface features such as grammar and wording or deeper features such as ideas, organization, and coherence. Ask the reviewer to focus feedback on that target, revise at the same level, and use a separate pass when the other level also matters.
entries.action: Before asking for feedback on a student or learning-focused draft, choose the current revision target. Use a surface pass for grammar, spelling, wording, and similar features; use a deep pass for ideas, organization, coherence, or other meaning-level features. Tell the reviewer which level you want them to focus on, revise against that target, and run a separate pass if the other level also needs work.
entries.check_in: What was the revision target for this pass, and did the feedback actually help you revise at that level?

entries.title: Build Toward a Weekly Movement Baseline
entries.description: Plan how ordinary walking, moderate activity, vigorous activity or strength work can fit your week. Adapt the plan to your abilities and medical guidance rather than forcing one routine.
entries.action: Look at the coming week, mark the activity you already do, then add realistic walking, moderate or vigorous activity, and strength sessions where they fit. Build gradually rather than treating the guideline as a one-day target.
entries.check_in: Does the plan fit your current ability, schedule and any guidance from your health professional? Adjust it rather than forcing a target that is inappropriate for you.

entries.title: Make a Specific Repair Attempt After a Workable Conflict
entries.description: After a misunderstanding or conflict where it is safe to re-engage, make a specific repair attempt: name what you did, acknowledge the likely impact without arguing about intent, apologize for your part, offer a concrete corrective action, and invite the other person's view. Do not demand forgiveness or immediate reconciliation.
entries.action: Wait until you can speak without escalating. Name the specific action or words you are taking responsibility for. Acknowledge the impact as you understand it without using your intention to cancel the other person's experience. Apologize for your part without an 'if'. Offer one concrete repair or behavior change you can actually make, then ask how the other person sees it. Listen to the answer. Do not require forgiveness, agreement, or immediate trust in return.
entries.check_in: Did I own a specific part without defending it, offer a realistic repair, and give the other person room to respond or decline?

entries.title: Let AI Draft Routine Replies, Keep the Human on the Conversation
entries.description: For repetitive support or service messages, AI can propose a response from the case facts and approved guidance while the human checks diagnosis, policy, tone, and the actual next step. Large-scale field evidence supports gains in one customer-support setting, especially for less experienced workers.
entries.action: Provide only information you are allowed to share, plus the customer question and approved policy or knowledge source. Ask for a concise draft. Check that it answers the real issue, does not invent policy or status, and gives the correct next action before sending.
entries.check_in: Did the suggestion save wording effort while leaving the human more attentive to the customer's actual problem?

entries.title: Batch Non-Urgent Notifications Instead of Receiving Them All Day
entries.description: Group non-urgent smartphone notifications into a few predictable delivery windows while keeping genuinely urgent channels available. The useful idea is predictable batching, not a magic number of batches.
entries.action: Choose the apps whose alerts are useful but rarely urgent. Use your phone's notification summary, scheduled focus mode, or another reversible setting to deliver those alerts in predictable windows. Keep calls, selected contacts, security alerts, calendars, or other genuinely time-sensitive channels outside the batch. Start with a schedule that fits your day rather than copying the study's three-times-a-day condition as a universal rule.
entries.check_in: Did I feel interrupted less often without creating missed urgent information, compulsive manual checking, or anxiety about what I could not see?

entries.title: Action and Mood Observation Note
entries.description: Use a short note to compare an activity with what you noticed before and after it. Treat the note as observation, not proof that an activity caused a mood change.
entries.action: Write the situation, the activity you chose, how you felt before, and how you felt afterward. Add one alternative explanation so the note does not turn correlation into certainty.
entries.check_in: What did you observe, and what would be worth trying or discussing next without assuming the activity caused the change?

entries.title: Try Short High-Intensity Intervals Safely
entries.description: Perform a HIIT session with 20 seconds of intense exercise (like sprinting or jumping jacks) followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated for 8 rounds.
entries.action: If vigorous exercise is appropriate for your current fitness and health, choose a simple movement you can perform safely. You can use it as one short interval session, or as brief exercise snacks separated across the day when a full workout is unlikely. Make the effort challenging but controlled. Treat 20/10, 3 × 1 minute, 4 × 1 minute and similar timers as formats to adapt, not scientifically optimized doses.
entries.check_in: Was the effort genuinely challenging but still controlled, could I repeat it without losing movement quality, and over several weeks is fitness or function trending in a useful direction rather than just my streak count?

entries.title: Check Email in Deliberate Windows Instead of Continuously
entries.description: If constant inbox checking fragments your day, test a few deliberate email windows and close the inbox between them. Match the schedule to real response expectations rather than copying a fixed number from a study.
entries.action: Choose a small number of email windows that still meet the real response expectations of your work and personal life. Close or hide the inbox between those windows and disable nonessential email alerts. Keep a separate urgent channel for issues that genuinely cannot wait. Do not treat three checks per day as a universal rule; that was the experimental condition, not an optimized schedule.
entries.check_in: Was my day less stressful or fragmented, did I miss anything genuinely time-sensitive, and did I compensate by manually reopening the inbox anyway?

entries.title: Use AI to Widen the Option Set, Not Make the Decision
entries.description: When a decision feels binary or prematurely settled, ask AI for plausible alternatives, missing criteria, and arguments against your current favorite. Verify factual claims independently and keep the final weighting of trade-offs human.
entries.action: Write your objective, constraints, and current leading option. Ask AI for materially different alternatives, missing criteria, and the strongest case against your favorite. Verify any external facts, then compare options using your own criteria and downside limits. Do not ask the model to hide the trade-off inside a single confident recommendation.
entries.check_in: Did AI reveal an option, criterion, or counterargument I had missed without becoming the authority that decides what I value?

entries.title: Before You Commit to a Judgment, Consider the Opposite
entries.description: When a judgment matters and you already feel convinced, deliberately generate a plausible explanation, evidence pattern, or outcome that would point the other way. Use it as a bias check, not as a rule to distrust every conclusion.
entries.action: Write your current conclusion in one sentence. Then ask: what evidence, mechanism, or alternative explanation could make the opposite conclusion reasonable? Generate a concrete alternative rather than telling yourself to be objective. Check whether your decision would change if that alternative were true. Use this on decisions where biased assimilation or one-sided hypothesis testing is a real risk; do not turn it into endless doubt about routine choices.
entries.check_in: What plausible disconfirming case did I generate, and did it reveal a missing fact, a weak assumption, or no meaningful reason to change course?

entries.title: Specific Gratitude Note
entries.description: Write one to three specific things you appreciated and why they mattered. Keep the practice optional and factual; gratitude is not a requirement to feel positive or a substitute for care.
entries.action: Choose one to three concrete moments, people, resources or actions from the day. Write what happened and one sentence about why it mattered to you. Skip the practice when it feels forced or unhelpful.
entries.check_in: Did the note help you notice something specific, or did it feel mechanical, invalidating, or like another obligation? Keep, change, or drop it accordingly.

entries.title: Move Caffeine Earlier When Sleep Matters
entries.description: If caffeine may be reaching into the night, move the last dose earlier and reduce large late-day doses. A 2025 randomized crossover trial found that a single 400 mg dose disrupted several sleep measures even when taken many hours before bed; a small 100 mg dose did not show a significant effect at the tested timings. That is a reason to be dose-aware, not a license for one universal cutoff.
entries.action: For one or two weeks, note the time and rough amount of your last caffeine, your bedtime, and whether sleep onset, overnight restfulness, and next-day sleepiness are broadly better or worse. Start by moving the last large dose earlier or reducing it; do not deliberately take caffeine late just to test your tolerance.
entries.check_in: When was my last caffeine, roughly how much was it, and did sleep and next-day alertness look better, worse, or unchanged across several days?

entries.title: Use AI to Widen the Idea Set Before You Choose
entries.description: When you are stuck on the first obvious idea, use AI to generate alternatives across different assumptions or constraints. Experimental evidence suggests generative AI can raise judged creativity in some ideation tasks; it does not decide which idea fits your real context.
entries.action: State the problem and constraints. Ask for several directions that must differ from one another in a named way. Cluster similar answers, discard obvious filler, and evaluate the remaining options against real constraints and evidence.
entries.check_in: Did AI add genuinely different options, or merely rephrase the same idea several times?

entries.title: Make Your Phone Less Visually Tempting with Grayscale
entries.description: If you want to spend less time on your phone, try switching the display to grayscale for a bounded trial. Treat it as friction against habitual use, not as a productivity, sleep, or mental-health upgrade.
entries.action: Enable grayscale on your phone and leave the rest of your normal setup alone for a bounded trial. Use the phone when you actually need it; the point is not abstinence. Notice whether automatic checking becomes less attractive. If color is important for navigation, accessibility, work, photos, or another real task, switch color back on for that task instead of treating grayscale as a purity test.
entries.check_in: Did my phone screen time or automatic checking change, and did I simply move the same distraction to another device?

entries.title: Deliberate Attention Switching with Everyday Sounds
entries.description: Use several neutral sounds around you to practice deliberately selecting one sound, switching to another, and then noticing several at once. Treat this as an attention-flexibility drill, not a treatment for worry, anxiety, or another condition.
entries.action: Find a safe place with several ordinary sounds. Attend closely to one sound without needing to block the others. Deliberately switch to a second and then a third sound. Finish by broadening attention so several sounds can be noticed together. Keep the exercise brief and stop when you choose.
entries.check_in: Could you intentionally select, switch, and broaden attention? Record the skill you practiced, not whether worry or another symptom changed.

entries.title: Use a High-Intensity Interval Timer Safely
entries.description: Follow the Tabata protocol: 20 seconds of very intense exercise (like burpees or mountain climbers) followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated for 4 minutes (8 rounds).
entries.action: If very vigorous exercise is suitable for you, use an interval timer to alternate a short period of harder work with recovery. A 20-second work and 10-second recovery pattern can be one option, but choose a movement and number of rounds you can control safely rather than treating 8 all-out rounds as mandatory.
entries.check_in: What movement and interval did I use, was the effort appropriate for my fitness today, did I maintain control, and was there any pain or reason to stop?

entries.title: Summarize with AI, Then Reconcile Against the Source
entries.description: For a long document you are allowed to process, ask AI for a structured summary tied to the source, then verify the claims that will affect a decision, message, or deliverable. The summary is navigation; the source remains the authority.
entries.action: Provide only material you are permitted to share. Ask for a summary with sections, explicit uncertainties, and source locations when available. Mark the claims that affect your decision, then open the source and verify those claims directly before reusing them.
entries.check_in: Can I point from every important statement in my final output back to the original source rather than to the AI summary?

entries.title: Turn a Good Intention into an If-Then Plan
entries.description: Turn a repeated low-stakes choice into a simple cue-and-action rule, add a fallback for common exceptions, and revise the rule when it creates friction or no longer fits the work.
entries.action: Choose one repeated situation, describe the cue in observable terms, choose a small action you can safely perform when the cue appears, add a fallback for a common exception, use the rule when the situation occurs, and revise or retire it when it stops fitting the work.
entries.check_in: Did the cue occur, did I follow the chosen action, what exception appeared, and should the rule stay, change, or be removed?

entries.title: Practice Facing a Small Fear Gradually
entries.description: When facing a fear, remind yourself that you’re safe. Repeat phrases like, ‘I am safe,’ ‘This is just a feeling,’ or ‘I can handle this.’
entries.action: Choose one situation you avoid because it feels frightening but that is not actually dangerous. Break it into smaller steps, start with a manageable step, approach it gradually, and notice what happens rather than trying to force fear away with a required phrase or ritual.
entries.check_in: What step did I try, how difficult did it feel before and after, what did I learn, and what would be a sensible next step?

entries.title: Benchmark AI on the Task Before You Trust the Workflow
entries.description: AI performance is uneven across tasks that can look similarly difficult. Before redesigning a workflow around a model, run it on representative cases, score the outputs against a human-defined standard, and identify where human review is still mandatory.
entries.action: Choose a small sample containing easy, ordinary, and awkward cases. Define what counts as acceptable before running the model. Compare AI output with the source or a trusted human result, record failure patterns, and decide which cases can be assisted, which need review, and which should stay human-first.
entries.check_in: Do I know the cases where AI is reliable enough to help and the cases where its polished answer should not be trusted?

entries.title: Walk Soon After a Meal When You Would Otherwise Sit
entries.description: When it is safe and practical, replace some sitting after a meal with comfortable walking. Evidence supports an acute effect on post-meal glucose, not a universal walking dose or long-term treatment claim.
entries.action: After a meal, choose an ordinary walk that feels comfortable and fits the situation. Starting relatively soon after eating matches the direction of the reviewed acute evidence better than deliberately waiting a long time, but Brali does not prescribe a universal minute mark, pace, or duration. If you use glucose-lowering medication, have a condition affected by exercise or meals, or have been given specific activity advice, follow your clinical plan instead of using this page as treatment guidance.
entries.check_in: Did the walk replace sitting without causing discomfort or disrupting a medical plan, and is it practical enough to repeat when useful?

entries.title: Pause Before Acting on a High-Stress Urge
entries.description: When a situation is safe enough to pause, notice the urge to react, describe what is happening, choose a harmless short delay, and then reassess the next action. This is not full DBT or crisis care.
entries.action: Pause. Describe the situation in one factual sentence and name the action urge without judging it. Choose a harmless brief activity that creates time rather than escalating the situation. Then reassess what action is safest and most useful.
entries.check_in: Did you create a pause without making the situation worse, and what safe next action did you choose? Do not score success by whether the emotion disappeared.

entries.title: Leave a Ready-to-Resume Note Before You Switch Tasks
entries.description: When you must leave unfinished work, capture where you stopped, the next concrete action, and one critical restart detail before switching. The goal is a cleaner return, not eliminating every cost of interruption.
entries.action: Use this only when unfinished work is about to be interrupted or deliberately parked. Before switching, capture three pieces of information in whatever format fits the task: your current state, the next concrete action, and one critical detail or open question that would otherwise have to be reconstructed. Then switch. When you return, read the note and start from the recorded next action rather than re-scanning the entire task.
entries.check_in: When I returned, could I identify the next action quickly, or did I still have to reconstruct the task from scratch?

entries.title: Attempt First, Use AI for Feedback, Retest Without It
entries.description: For learning tasks, make a genuine attempt before asking AI to explain, critique, or extend your work, then reproduce the target skill without assistance. Recent evidence on generative AI in education is mixed enough that the workflow should preserve learner activity rather than assume the chatbot itself improves learning.
entries.action: Name the skill you are actually trying to acquire. Attempt a problem, explanation, translation, derivation, or answer unaided. Ask AI to identify gaps, give a contrasting example, or explain one sticking point. Check the feedback against trusted material when accuracy matters, then perform a fresh attempt without AI.
entries.check_in: Can I now perform or explain the target skill without leaning on the AI output?

entries.title: Draft Professional Writing with AI, Then Take Back the Edit
entries.description: For routine professional writing, give AI the purpose, audience, constraints, and source facts, ask for a draft, then revise it yourself. Controlled evidence supports productivity gains for some professional writing tasks, not automatic accuracy or judgment.
entries.action: Provide the audience, goal, source facts, must-include points, and constraints. Ask for one draft. Compare it with the source material, remove invented details, restore your own judgment and voice, and send only the version you can defend without the model in the room.
entries.check_in: Did AI reduce drafting time without introducing claims, tone, or commitments I would not have written myself?

entries.title: Try Progressive Muscle Relaxation Gently
entries.description: Tightly squeeze each muscle group for five seconds, then relax it for thirty seconds, moving from your toes up to your head.
entries.action: Sit or lie somewhere comfortable and work through a few muscle groups one at a time. Gently tense each group for no more than about five seconds, then release it and notice the contrast. Do not strain, and skip or release any area that causes significant discomfort. If sleep is your target, use PMR as a repeatable wind-down experiment rather than a one-night sleep test.
entries.check_in: Did I practise without pain or straining? If I am using PMR for sleep, across several attempts did winding down or my subjective sleep feel meaningfully easier, unchanged, or worse?

entries.title: Talk About a Fear With Someone You Trust
entries.description: Share your fears with a trusted friend, family member, or therapist.
entries.action: Choose someone you trust and tell them, in your own words, what you are worried or afraid about. You can also say what kind of support you want, such as listening, practical help, or simply company. Keep the conversation within boundaries that feel appropriate for both of you.
entries.check_in: Who did I talk to, what did I want from the conversation, did I feel heard or supported, and is there any next step I need?

entries.title: Pair a Useful Task with Something You Genuinely Want
entries.description: Pair a beneficial activity that is easy to postpone with a compatible pleasure you already enjoy. Temptation bundling has field-experiment support for exercise, but it is not a universal habit formula and effects can fade.
entries.action: Choose one 'should' behavior that is useful but easy to delay and one 'want' experience that can happen at the same time without making the task worse. Examples might include a favorite audiobook during a walk or routine cardio, a preferred podcast while doing repetitive household work, or another compatible pairing. If you want a stronger commitment device, reserve that entertainment for the target activity. Keep the pairing safe: do not add absorbing media to driving, technical work, strength movements that require concentration, or any task where divided attention creates risk.
entries.check_in: Did the pairing make the useful activity easier to start or repeat, and did the reward stay enjoyable without damaging the quality or safety of the task?

entries.title: Try a Short Breath Meditation
entries.description: Sit somewhere safe, let your breathing stay natural, notice when attention wanders, and bring it back. Five minutes is a convenient container, not a therapeutic dose or a test of whether you are good at calming down.
entries.action: Sit somewhere comfortable and safe. Let breathing stay natural. Notice the sensations of breathing; when attention drifts into plans, memories, sounds or commentary, notice that and return to the breath without grading yourself. Use five minutes only if it is a convenient starting container. After several attempts, keep the practice only if it is useful for you.
entries.check_in: Did I notice attention wandering and return without turning it into a fight? Was the practice useful, neutral or uncomfortable? Would another wellbeing practice fit me better today?

entries.title: Ask a Few Questions Before You Start Learning
entries.description: Before reading, watching, or studying new material, try a few questions about the specific information you want to learn. Attempt an answer, then study and check it. Evidence supports better learning for the prequestioned information, not a general boost to everything else.
entries.action: Choose a small set of questions that point to information you genuinely want to learn. Before opening the explanation, reading the chapter, or watching the lesson, make a brief attempt at each answer even if you are unsure. Then study normally, paying attention when the material resolves those questions. Afterward, check the answers against the source. Use this to target important information, not as a claim that every unasked detail will also be learned better.
entries.check_in: After studying, can I answer the questions accurately without looking, and did the questions point me toward information that actually mattered?

entries.title: Pause Long Enough to Notice a Good Moment
entries.description: When something genuinely pleasant is already happening, give it a little deliberate attention instead of rushing past it. This is a conservative savoring practice, not a rule to feel positive or reinterpret difficult experiences.
entries.action: Choose a positive experience that is already real: a good meal, a joke, a quiet walk, finishing useful work, music, a kind message, or another ordinary moment. For a short period, stop adding new input. Notice one or two concrete details and what makes the moment worth noticing. Then continue your day. Do not use the exercise to deny an unpleasant feeling or to manufacture gratitude for something that is not good.
entries.check_in: Did I actually stay with a positive experience for a moment, and did the practice feel useful, neutral, awkward, or forced?

entries.title: Make Goal Progress Visible Instead of Guessing
entries.description: For a goal you are actively pursuing, choose one observable progress signal, record it at useful checkpoints, compare it with the target, and use the result to adjust the next action. Monitoring helps when it informs action; more tracking is not automatically better.
entries.action: Choose one goal where feedback can still change what you do. Pick one observable indicator that is close to the real outcome or behavior you care about. Record it at checkpoints that match the task, compare it with the target or previous checkpoint, and decide one adjustment. Prefer a small trace you will actually use over a dashboard full of decorative metrics.
entries.check_in: What changed in the progress signal, and what is the one next action that follows from that information?

entries.title: Use AI to Scaffold Code, Then Make Tests Decide
entries.description: Use AI to produce a first implementation for a bounded coding task, then inspect the diff, run tests, add missing edge cases, and reject code you cannot explain. A controlled experiment found faster completion on one coding task; it did not establish universal software quality gains.
entries.action: Define the behavior and constraints first. Ask AI for a small implementation. Read the diff, run the existing test suite, add tests for edge cases and failure paths, and inspect security or data-handling implications. Keep only code you can explain and maintain.
entries.check_in: Did AI shorten implementation time without increasing code I do not understand, test, or want to own?

entries.title: Explain What You Just Learned in Your Own Words
entries.description: After a meaningful chunk of digital learning, pause and explain the idea, relationship, or step in your own words, then compare with the source and correct gaps. Meta-analytic evidence supports self-explanation in digital learning, with meaningful variation across contexts and material types.
entries.action: Study a manageable chunk, then look away from the explanation and produce a brief self-explanation: what the idea means, why a step follows, how it connects to what you already know, or when it would apply. Compare your explanation with the source, identify one gap or error, and revise it. Use the prompts that fit the material; do not turn every paragraph into a compulsory monologue.
entries.check_in: Can I explain the idea accurately enough to reconstruct the key relationship or step, and what did I have to correct after checking the source?

entries.title: Comfortable Diaphragmatic Breathing
entries.description: Try a few slow, comfortable breaths while noticing the abdomen move. Keep the exercise easy, stop if it feels uncomfortable, and do not use it instead of medical care.
entries.action: Sit or lie in a comfortable position, let the breath slow without forcing a count, notice the abdomen rise and fall, and stop after a few easy cycles or whenever you prefer.
entries.check_in: Did the exercise feel comfortable and leave you ready for the next ordinary action? Stop if you feel dizzy, short of breath, distressed, or otherwise unwell.

entries.title: Separate Review Sessions Instead of Cramming
entries.description: For verbal material you need to recall later, divide repeated study across separate sessions instead of concentrating the same planned review into one sitting. Choose the gap in relation to the intended retention period, then check recall and adjust rather than following one universal schedule.
entries.action: Choose one set of verbal material and decide how long you need to retain it. Split the planned repetitions across at least two sessions separated by time. Use a longer gap when the required retention period is longer, then check final recall and adjust the next schedule instead of treating one interval as universally optimal.
entries.check_in: Did I separate the study episodes rather than cram them together, and did the chosen gap fit the period over which I needed to remember the material?

entries.title: Turn a Screen-Free Meeting Into a Walking Meeting
entries.description: Use a walking meeting to replace part of a long sitting block when the conversation does not require a screen. Evidence supports the movement break, not a special meeting effect.
entries.action: When a meeting is mostly listening and talking, replace some of that sitting with an easy walk if the route, weather, privacy and meeting format make it safe. Keep screen-heavy or safety-critical conversations seated. Capture decisions before you finish.
entries.check_in: Did I replace a sitting block with walking without making the meeting worse? Was the route safe and the conversation easy enough to follow? Would I use this format again for this kind of meeting?

entries.title: Translate a Problem into a Nature-Inspired Design Principle
entries.description: Describe the function a solution must perform, inspect a biological example, extract a transferable principle and test one safe application without copying the organism literally.
entries.action: State what the solution must do without naming the current solution. Choose a biological example from a reliable description. Separate the observed structure or process from the metaphor. Write one transferable principle, generate several applications and test the smallest reversible option within safety and operational constraints.
entries.check_in: What function did I study, what principle did I extract, and what did the small test reveal about its usefulness or limit?

entries.title: Short Resilience Reminder
entries.description: Create a short phrase that acknowledges difficulty without pretending it is easy, then points back to one action you can still control.
entries.action: Write one sentence in the form: This is difficult, and the next thing I can control is ___. Keep it specific to the current situation.
entries.check_in: Did the phrase lead to a concrete action, or did it become empty motivation that you repeated without changing anything?

entries.title: Use an Extreme Seed, Then Return to Reality
entries.description: Start an idea session with a deliberately unrealistic seed, explore its consequences without defending it and then translate useful fragments back into real constraints.
entries.action: State the real problem. Choose an extreme seed that changes one constraint, customer, resource or rule. During a short generation round, list consequences and variants without arguing with the seed. Remove the seed, restore actual constraints and choose one feasible fragment to test or develop.
entries.check_in: Which useful fragment came from the extreme seed, and what real constraint or next test made it actionable?

entries.title: Automatic Savings Rule
entries.description: If essential obligations are covered, automate a modest transfer to savings and review whether the amount remains comfortable. This is general educational guidance, not individualized financial advice.
entries.action: Review upcoming essential expenses, choose a small transfer amount you can change or cancel, schedule it after income arrives, and check that it does not create a shortfall.
entries.check_in: Did the automation make saving easier without making bills, debt payments, or necessary spending harder to cover?

entries.title: Write a Context Brief Before Drafting
entries.description: Before drafting, write a compact brief that identifies the primary reader, where the text will appear, what the reader should understand or do, which constraints apply, and what facts or sources must be verified.
entries.action: Write the primary reader, publication surface, desired reader action or understanding, required tone or format constraints, facts that must be checked, and any detail that should be omitted for privacy, confidentiality or scope. Then build the outline from that brief.
entries.check_in: Who is this for, where will it appear, what should the reader understand or do, and which constraint or fact must the draft respect?

entries.title: Organize Complex Information Around One Decision
entries.description: Define the audience and decision, group related material into labeled parts, put the main path in a useful order, and move supporting detail into linked layers instead of either flattening everything or presenting every detail at once.
entries.action: Name the primary audience and the decision or action they need to understand. Group related material by purpose, give each group a descriptive label, order the groups into a main path, and move supporting definitions, examples, calculations or source detail into a layer that remains easy to retrieve.
entries.check_in: What does the audience need to decide or do, which groups form the main path, what belongs in supporting detail, and can a reader find that detail when needed?

entries.title: Shared-Value Option Map
entries.description: Map what each side values, where constraints differ, and which exchanges could create value without pretending every conflict has a win-win solution.
entries.action: List what each side wants, what each side can trade at relatively low cost, and two or three options that combine those differences. Then test the options with the other side.
entries.check_in: Did the conversation uncover a real trade, or are the interests still incompatible enough that a clear boundary or no-deal option is better?

entries.title: Structure Dense Writing for Fast Navigation
entries.description: Turn a dense draft into a navigable document by giving each section one job and choosing headings, tables, diagrams, or images according to the information the reader needs to inspect.
entries.action: Name the reader's main task, read the current headings without the body, reorganize sections around that path, replace repeated comparisons with a table when rows share the same attributes, use a diagram for relationships or sequence, and keep images only when they show information that prose would make harder to inspect.
entries.check_in: Can a reader scan the headings and understand the path, and does every visual element answer a question that the surrounding text does not answer as clearly?

entries.title: Leave Useful Feedback
entries.description: Write feedback that separates what happened, why it mattered to you, and what change would make the experience better.
entries.action: Describe one concrete thing that worked or failed, explain the effect it had on your task, and add one specific suggestion if you have one.
entries.check_in: Could the recipient understand what happened and what might improve without guessing what you meant?

entries.title: Keep a Work Wins Log You Can Reuse
entries.description: Record completed work, solved problems, decisions, useful contributions and recoveries in a compact log so you can retrieve concrete examples for reviews, resumes, proposals, retrospectives and planning.
entries.action: After a meaningful piece of work, add a short entry with the situation, your contribution, the concrete result or current state, and one or two tags. During a review, retrieve entries that match the purpose and verify any figures or claims before reusing them.
entries.check_in: What changed, what did I contribute, what detail will I need later, and is the entry specific enough to reuse without exaggeration?

entries.title: Use One Constraint to Produce a Different Creative Draft
entries.description: When open-ended exploration is producing more browsing than making, choose one reversible constraint on scope, tools, format, or time and use it to create a concrete alternative you can compare with the original direction.
entries.action: Name the artifact and the part that feels too open, choose one constraint that does not violate the brief, create a reversible variant without adding new constraints midstream, compare the result with the original requirements, and keep only the useful difference.
entries.check_in: What did I constrain, what changed in the artifact, and did the constraint reveal anything worth keeping?

entries.title: Run a Short, Concrete Information Interview
entries.description: Ask permission, focus on one recent event, follow the sequence step by step and separate remembered facts, estimates and interpretation.
entries.action: Explain why you are asking and get permission. Ask the person to walk through the most recent relevant example. Use one question at a time about sequence, context, tools, decisions and uncertainty. Summarize what you heard and invite correction.
entries.check_in: What concrete sequence did I learn, what remains an estimate or interpretation, and what did the person correct?

entries.title: Connect a General Point to a Concrete Example
entries.description: State the general point, add a concrete example or observable detail that belongs to it, connect the example back to the point, and remove specifics that do not help the audience understand the message or next action.
entries.action: Write the main point in plain language, choose an example, observation, step or verified figure that illustrates it, explain the connection in one sentence, and remove details that do not change understanding or action. If you began with a detail, reverse the sequence by stating the broader point it supports.
entries.check_in: What is the general point, which concrete detail makes it easier to understand, what does that detail show here, and which specifics can be removed without changing the meaning?

entries.title: Screen Break Checkpoint
entries.description: Use a simple checkpoint during screen-heavy work: look away, change posture, and decide whether the next block still deserves your attention.
entries.action: At a natural breakpoint in a long screen session, look away from the display, relax your posture, and name the next task before returning.
entries.check_in: Did the pause make the next action clearer, or did it reveal that you should stop, switch, or rest?

entries.title: One Move, Several Benefits
entries.description: Look for one concrete action that advances two compatible priorities, then check that combining them does not make the action vague or overloaded.
entries.action: Name two priorities, brainstorm one concrete action that can serve both, and reject the combination if it makes either priority weaker or unclear.
entries.check_in: Did combining the priorities simplify the plan, or did it create a compromised task that serves neither one well?

entries.title: Stay Sharp: - Take Notes: Write Down Key Points from the Person Speaking Before
entries.description: To stay sharp: - Take notes: Write down key points from the person speaking before you. - Breathe and listen: Avoid rehearsing your own response while someone else is speaking. - Repeat mentally: After someone speaks, quickly repeat their main point in your head. Example: In a team meeting, note what the person before you says and reference it when it’s your turn.
entries.action: To stay sharp: - Take notes: Write down key points from the person speaking before you. - Breathe and listen: Avoid rehearsing your own response while someone else is speaking. - Repeat mentally: After someone speaks, quickly repeat their main point in your head. Example: In a team meeting, note what the person before you says and reference it when it’s your turn.
entries.check_in: Check in when you stay present during group conversations and recall the last speaker's points.

entries.title: Rehearse a Difficult Conversation with AI Before the Real One
entries.description: Before a difficult but ordinary conversation, use AI to role-play several plausible reactions, practise a concise opening, and identify points where you may become unclear or defensive. Treat the simulation as rehearsal, not as a model of the other person's mind.
entries.action: State the goal, your opening, and relevant context without unnecessary private detail. Ask AI to play a neutral, skeptical, and confused counterpart. Practise responding with facts, boundaries, and questions. Write one shorter opening after the rehearsal and use that in the real conversation if it still fits.
entries.check_in: Am I better prepared to listen and respond, or did I start treating the simulated person's reaction as a prediction?

entries.title: Automate a Routine Report with Validation and Fallback
entries.description: Automate a stable reporting workflow only after defining source ownership, transformations, validation rules, freshness, failure handling, and a manual fallback.
entries.action: Map the report consumer, source data, transformations and delivery step. Define validation rules for schema, completeness, freshness and key totals. Build a small automated path with logging and a visible failure state, keep a manual fallback, and stop publication when validation fails.
entries.check_in: Did the automated report use the expected source, pass validation, arrive on time, and fail visibly when an assumption broke?

entries.title: Pause a Heated Disagreement and Test One Claim
entries.description: Slow down a defensive exchange, restate the other person's claim, identify what could change either view and choose one concrete check or a respectful stopping point.
entries.action: Notice that you are defending rather than examining. Pause before replying. Restate the other person's claim in words they accept, then state your own position and uncertainty. Ask what information would change either view. Choose one concrete check, or stop when the exchange is no longer productive or safe.
entries.check_in: What claim did we clarify, what could change either view, and did we choose a check, revise a position or stop respectfully?

entries.title: Rehearse One Real Language Scenario
entries.description: Choose a real low-risk interaction in the language you are learning, prepare the minimum useful phrases plus a repair phrase, rehearse likely turns, try the interaction when appropriate, and update the phrase set from what was difficult.
entries.action: Define the scenario and desired outcome, write the core request or response, add likely follow-up phrases and one repair phrase for misunderstanding, rehearse both sides aloud, use the interaction when appropriate, and update the phrase set from the point where you hesitated or needed clarification.
entries.check_in: Which scenario did I rehearse, where did the interaction become difficult, which phrase or listening cue should I add, and what can I reuse next time?

entries.title: Audit Workspace Friction Before Buying More Gear
entries.description: Inspect where a workspace makes the actual task harder to see, reach, switch, connect, or reset; change one layout variable; and keep the change only when it removes friction without creating a new problem.
entries.action: Choose one frequent task, walk through it slowly, note every unnecessary reach, obstruction, visibility issue, cable move, device swap, or reset, rank the friction points, change one reversible layout variable, use the task again, and keep or undo the change based on what became easier or harder.
entries.check_in: Which step in the task had avoidable friction, what single workspace change did I make, and did it remove that friction without moving the problem somewhere else?

entries.title: Use One Random Constraint to Break a Creative Stalemate
entries.description: When familiar approaches keep producing the same result, draw or select one bounded prompt, create a reversible alternative for a few minutes, and keep only the part that improves the actual work.
entries.action: Name the part of the work that feels stuck, select one prompt or constraint without hunting for the perfect one, create a separate reversible version under that constraint, stop after one useful pass, compare it with the original, and keep only the changes that improve the brief.
entries.check_in: What constraint did I try, what changed in the artifact, and which part—if any—is worth carrying into the real version?

entries.title: AI-Assisted Premortem
entries.description: Use an AI model as a brainstorming partner for possible failure modes, then verify important risks against the real plan before choosing mitigations.
entries.action: Describe the plan without sensitive information, ask an AI for plausible ways it could fail, group the suggestions, verify the important ones yourself, and choose mitigations only for risks that survive the check.
entries.check_in: Which risks were genuinely relevant after verification, and which model suggestions were generic, impossible, or based on missing context?

entries.title: Expect the Unexpected
entries.description: When predicting trends: - Ask yourself: "Could there be sudden changes or breaks in this trend?" - Prepare for shifts: Always consider outliers and unexpected events in planning. - Look for weak signals: Early signs of change can help you adapt quickly. Example: A stock steadily rising? Plan for a downturn just as much as for continued growth.
entries.action: When predicting trends: - Ask yourself: "Could there be sudden changes or breaks in this trend?" - Prepare for shifts: Always consider outliers and unexpected events in planning. - Look for weak signals: Early signs of change can help you adapt quickly. Example: A stock steadily rising? Plan for a downturn just as much as for continued growth.
entries.check_in: Check in when you account for potential trend breaks in your planning.

entries.title: Check Whether a Streak Changes the Next Event
entries.description: Before acting on a streak, identify whether earlier outcomes can change the next event and use a pre-defined decision rule rather than a story about what is due.
entries.action: Describe the next event and the recent streak. Ask what carries information or state from earlier outcomes into the next one. If there is no connection, ignore the streak and use the same probability or decision rule. If a connection may exist, identify the relevant state and gather that information. Use a pre-defined stop rule for repeated high-cost decisions.
entries.check_in: What connection did I identify between past and next events, and did my action follow the rule or merely the feeling that an outcome was due?

entries.title: Decompose a Hard Problem with TRIZ-Inspired Contradictions
entries.description: Describe the unwanted result, expose the trade-off or contradiction, split the system into parts, and check a change that removes a constraint instead of merely optimizing around it.
entries.action: State the unwanted outcome, map the main parts and interactions, write the trade-off as two requirements that appear to conflict, generate separation or redesign options, choose a reversible check, and record which assumption or constraint changed.
entries.check_in: What contradiction did I expose, what separation or redesign did I check, and did it remove the conflict or only move it elsewhere?

entries.title: Use a Short Phrase to Choose the Next Step
entries.description: Use a brief phrase as a cue to acknowledge a difficult moment and choose one small, controllable action. The phrase is a reminder, not a prediction about how the situation will end.
entries.action: When you feel stuck, pause and repeat a short phrase once. Name what is difficult in plain language, then choose one action that is small enough to begin now. Skip the phrase if it feels hollow, pressuring or unrelated to the real problem.
entries.check_in: What was difficult, what action did I choose, and did the phrase help me begin or should I use a different cue next time?

entries.title: Replace grand claims with a grounded statement and one next action.
entries.description: Turn a vague positive statement into words you can presently stand behind, connect it to one action under your control, and revise the statement when it becomes false, empty, or unhelpful.
entries.action: Write the positive statement you are tempted to use, underline the part that feels exaggerated or outside your control, replace it with language you can currently stand behind, attach one concrete action that would be consistent with the statement, and review the wording after you act.
entries.check_in: Can I honestly endorse this statement now, what action does it point to, and should I keep, narrow, or replace the wording after seeing what I actually did?

entries.title: Give AI a Rubric and Ask for Specific Critique
entries.description: For a draft you own, give AI the purpose and a short rubric, ask it to point to specific places that miss the criteria, then decide which suggestions actually improve the work. Use critique as input, not as an automatic rewrite command.
entries.action: Write three to six criteria that describe a good result. Give the model the draft and rubric, ask for evidence from the draft for each criticism, and request no rewrite on the first pass. Triage the feedback, then make the changes you agree with.
entries.check_in: Did the critique point to observable gaps in the draft, or mostly produce generic advice I could paste onto any text?

entries.title: Extract a Table with AI, Then Sample-Check the Rows
entries.description: For repeated unstructured text you are allowed to process, ask AI to extract a fixed schema, include the source span for each row, and flag uncertainty. Then sample-check rows and fully verify fields that drive money, access, compliance, or other high-cost actions.
entries.action: Define the columns and allowed values before extraction. Ask the model to return null rather than guess, preserve a source snippet or locator for each row, and flag ambiguous cases. Check a random sample plus all high-impact rows against the original text before using the result downstream.
entries.check_in: Do I know the observed extraction error rate well enough for the consequence of the next step?

entries.title: Ask AI for Failure Cases Before You Ship
entries.description: Give AI a feature, process, calculation, message, or workflow and ask for edge cases and failure modes. Treat the output as a candidate list, deduplicate it, verify relevance, and convert the useful cases into executable tests or checklist items.
entries.action: Describe the intended behavior, constraints, known happy path, and expensive failures. Ask for boundary cases, invalid inputs, state transitions, concurrency or timing issues where relevant, and user misunderstandings. Remove duplicates, verify each candidate against the real system, and write tests for the cases worth keeping.
entries.check_in: Did AI expose a failure I had not covered, and did I turn that idea into a check rather than merely admire the list?

entries.title: Challenge Assumed Similarities
entries.description: When interacting with others: - Ask: "What’s unique about this person’s perspective or experience?" - Listen actively: Avoid projecting your own traits or beliefs onto them. - Reflect: Notice when you assume similarities without evidence and correct yourself. Example: Don’t assume a coworker has the same work style as you; ask about their preferences and needs.
entries.action: When interacting with others: - Ask: "What’s unique about this person’s perspective or experience?" - Listen actively: Avoid projecting your own traits or beliefs onto them. - Reflect: Notice when you assume similarities without evidence and correct yourself. Example: Don’t assume a coworker has the same work style as you; ask about their preferences and needs.
entries.check_in: Check in when you actively avoid assuming someone is just like you.

entries.title: Separate Observation from Human-Like Interpretation
entries.description: Describe what a non-human animal, plant, machine or model did before assigning a human motive. Add a system-specific alternative and state what remains uncertain.
entries.action: Choose one behavior or output. Record only what you could point to or reproduce. Write the human-like interpretation you first considered, then add a system-specific alternative and one low-risk way to check between them. Keep uncertainty visible when you cannot check.
entries.check_in: What did I directly observe, what interpretation did I add, and what alternative or check changed my next action?

entries.title: Write the Inclusion Rule Before Generalizing
entries.description: Record who or what entered an analysis, who was excluded and how the conclusion changes when missing cases are considered.
entries.action: State the question and population you want to understand. Record how cases entered the analysis, which cases were excluded or missing and whether selection depends on the outcome. Compare the conclusion with a broader view or label it as applying only to the selected group. Write what additional data would change the conclusion.
entries.check_in: Who was included, who was missing, and is my conclusion limited to the selected group or supported beyond it?

entries.title: Build a Support Map Around Specific Needs
entries.description: Map the kinds of support you sometimes need, identify appropriate people or communities for each kind, make specific requests that are easy to decline, and protect reciprocity and boundaries.
entries.action: Write down one current need, decide what kind of help would actually be useful, identify a person or community that is appropriate for that request, ask specifically and make declining easy, respect the answer, and record whether you need a different resource or a different kind of help next time.
entries.check_in: Was the request specific and appropriate, was the other person's boundary clear, and do I need to change the ask, the resource, or my own next action?

entries.title: Turn an AI Reflection into One Next Action
entries.description: Give an AI assistant a concrete goal, current constraints, and the decision you need to make; ask for options, assumptions, and failure modes; verify factual claims; then choose one reversible next action yourself.
entries.action: State one concrete goal or decision, provide the relevant constraints and what you already know, ask the AI for a small set of distinct options with assumptions and failure modes, challenge anything vague, verify factual claims that matter, choose one reversible next action yourself, and record what would cause you to change course.
entries.check_in: What became clearer, which AI claim still needs verification, what action did I choose, and what new information would make me revise the decision?

entries.title: Use Elimination Rules to Narrow a Decision
entries.description: Define a few decision constraints, eliminate options that clearly fail them, then compare the smaller remaining set without pretending arbitrary thresholds are universal rules.
entries.action: List the viable options, write two to four constraints that are genuinely relevant to this decision, eliminate only options that clearly fail a constraint, inspect what remains for missing information and trade-offs, then choose the next reversible test or decision step.
entries.check_in: Which constraint removed an option, what uncertainty remains among the survivors, and what is the smallest next step that would improve the decision?

entries.title: Explain One Idea with an Analogy and Its Limit
entries.description: Compare an unfamiliar idea with something familiar, state the matching point, name where the comparison stops and ask the listener to restate the idea.
entries.action: Write the idea you need to explain. Choose a familiar comparison, map only the important relationship, add one boundary sentence and ask the listener to restate the original idea. Revise the analogy if the restatement keeps the wrong detail.
entries.check_in: Could the listener restate the intended idea, and which part of the analogy clarified or distorted it?

entries.title: Ask for Feedback on One Specific Decision
entries.description: Give the reviewer context, ask one focused question, make the reply easy and decide what you will accept, test, discuss, defer or ignore.
entries.action: State the intended outcome and the current decision. Ask one focused question such as what is unclear, what assumption looks wrong or what should change first. Choose a reviewer who can judge that question, then record what you will accept, test, discuss, defer or ignore.
entries.check_in: What did I ask, what did the reviewer actually say, and what decision or test changed because of it?

entries.title: Run a Detail Check Before You Ship
entries.description: Inspect a concrete artifact against a small checklist, run a second pass from a different angle, log anomalies, and improve the checklist from real misses rather than training vague hypervigilance.
entries.action: Choose an artifact or environment where errors matter, write a short checklist from known failure modes, inspect once for completeness and once from a different perspective such as data consistency or user flow, record anomalies, fix them, and update the checklist when a new recurring miss appears.
entries.check_in: What defect or ambiguity did the check find, which checklist item caught it, and what recurring miss should change the next review?
